strengths: Formulates a novel and practical task: tuning-free transfer of time-varying visual effects from a reference video to target videos or images, addressing a clear limitation of text-prompt-based video editors.

Proposes an innovative, multi-source data generation pipeline (synthesizing paired videos via image editing, pose extraction, and conditional generation, combined with programmatic effects and LoRA adapters) to overcome the lack of paired training triplets for temporal effect transfer.

The model architecture is thoughtfully integrated into the Wan diffusion transformer backbone via spatial width-wise concatenation, accompanied by a multi-directional classifier-free guidance formulation that enables fine-grained user control over input vs. reference adherence at inference time.

Extensive experimental evaluation, featuring thorough user studies across three distinct tasks, quantitative similarity benchmarks with foundation video models (VideoPrism), and honest reporting of qualitative limitations.
weaknesses: High computational footprint at inference: concatenating reference video latents doubles the token length, resulting in long generation times (~7 minutes per 33-frame clip on an NVIDIA A100 GPU).

Dataset construction leans heavily toward human-centric scenarios due to reliance on pose extractors and the Senorita dataset, which may limit out-of-domain generalization to non-human subjects, complex physics/fluids, or expansive environmental camera shots.

Comparison against reference-guided video baselines is somewhat limited; while text-conditioned VACE and Lucy Edit are relevant, existing reference-guided video personalization/style transfer methods (e.g., StyleMaster or VideoAlchemy) were not directly compared against to empirically demonstrate the failure modes of static reference conditioning on temporal dynamics.

strengths: Novel and practically valuable task formulation: The paper tackles reference-based temporal visual effect transfer across videos without requiring test-time optimization or per-effect tuning, an important step beyond static style transfer or purely text-driven video editing.

Clever, multi-faceted dataset generation pipeline: Since paired training triplets (reference video, input video, target video) do not exist naturally, the authors design an automated synthesis strategy combining image editing, intermediate pose extraction, and conditional video interpolation, alongside LoRA-based and programmatic/code-based compositing (yielding over 120K triplets across 1,700 effects).

Effective conditioning architecture and flexible inference control: Extending the Wan DiT architecture with width-wise latent concatenation enables joint spatio-temporal self-attention across reference and target tokens. Furthermore, the decomposed multi-guidance formulation (text, reference, input) provides intuitive controllability over effect strength versus input preservation.

Comprehensive empirical validation: The method is evaluated across multiple modalities (I2V, V2V, code-based), supported by extensive user preference studies (RVA and IVA) and feature-space similarity metrics, showing strong generalization to unseen effects.
weaknesses: Inherent baseline disadvantage: Because existing video editing baselines (e.g., Wan VACE, Lucy Edit) are strictly text-driven or rely on static keyframe guidance, comparing them against a model receiving full reference video dynamics introduces an information asymmetry. Exploring adaptation of visual prompt/in-context video editing architectures (e.g., conditioning with visual tokens from the reference) as stronger reference-guided baselines would provide a more rigorous comparison.

Computational overhead at inference: Width-wise concatenation of reference latents doubles the sequence length in the diffusion transformer, increasing inference latency to ~7 minutes per 33-frame clip on an A100 GPU. Exploring cross-attention or compressed reference token representations could alleviate this cost.

Synthetic data bias and complex interaction artifacts: As noted in the limitations, the V2V pipeline relies on pose extraction and first/last frame generation, which inherently biases the model toward rigid or human pose-guided motions. The model struggles with non-rigid topological changes, fluid submergence, and fine-grained occlusions (e.g., Figure 9).

strengths: Pioneering and well-formulated task: The paper addresses a distinct and practical challenge in generative video editing—transferring dynamic, time-varying visual effects from a reference video onto target videos or images in a tuning-free, feed-forward manner, going beyond static style transfer or prompt-only editing.

Scalable and multi-faceted data generation pipeline: To overcome the absence of paired real-world video effect data, the authors design an automated curation pipeline combining LoRA-driven image-to-video generations, multi-stage generative V2V pairings (via image editing, pose extraction, and first-last frame generation), and programmatic compositing, yielding a rich dataset of over 120K triplets across 1,700 effects.

Effective conditioning design: The method extends the Wan diffusion transformer backbone cleanly by concatenating reference video latents along the spatial/width dimension and implementing hybrid latent masking, alongside multi-directional classifier-free guidance (CFG) for fine-grained control over input fidelity versus effect intensity.

Comprehensive perceptual validation: The paper conducts an extensive user preference study across multiple benchmarks (Neural V2V, Code-based V2V, and I2V) with over 1,300 total annotations, demonstrating strong human preference for the transferred effects over existing baselines.
weaknesses: Unbalanced baseline comparisons: Because existing open-source video editing methods do not natively condition on reference videos, all baselines (Wan VACE, Lucy Edit) are evaluated purely on text prompts describing the effect. While understandable due to the novelty of the setup, comparing a reference-conditioned model directly against text-only models inevitably biases reference adherence in favor of RefVFX; adapting concurrent in-context or multi-concept video frameworks as reference-guided baselines would provide a more rigorous benchmark.

Heavy reliance on synthetic and programmatic data: Roughly 100K of the 120K training triplets originate from relatively simplistic programmatic 2D transformations (e.g., posterization, pixelation, directional wipes) on segmented video masks, and the neural V2V subset relies on a complex cascade of generative models (text-to-image, image editing, pose estimation, and video generation). This introduces the risk of compounded synthesis artifacts and limits generalization to photorealistic, complex physical visual effects in the wild.

Substantial computational overhead: Width-wise concatenating full-length reference latents effectively doubles the spatial sequence length fed into the DiT attention blocks. This results in heavy inference costs (~7 minutes per 33-frame 480p clip on an NVIDIA A100 GPU), which significantly hinders practical adoption and interactive workflows.

Limited quantitative analysis and scene diversity: The quantitative evaluation primarily relies on VideoPrism/CLIP feature cosine similarities, which can be conflated by semantic content and global style rather than temporal dynamics. Furthermore, the training data and evaluations remain predominantly human-centric and foreground-focused, leaving open questions about performance on diverse camera motions, complex scenes, and severe occlusions (as acknowledged in the limitations).

strengths: Formulates an important, under-explored task in video editing: reference-based temporal visual effect transfer across videos without requiring per-concept test-time optimization.

Proposes a well-designed, scalable data generation pipeline combining three complementary sources (LoRA-based I2V clips, automated multi-stage pose-guided V2V pairs, and parameterized code-based compositing) to construct over 120K aligned triplets across 1,700 effects.

The conditioning architecture elegantly extends diffusion transformer latents width-wise for reference latents and channel-wise for input latents, supplemented by multi-directional classifier-free guidance for controllable trade-offs between input preservation and effect adherence.

Evaluations are rigorous, featuring a large-scale human preference study (>15,000 annotations from over 500 annotators), VideoPrism feature similarity metrics, and standard video generative benchmarks on unseen effect categories.
The paper is clearly written, well-organized, and candidly discusses current limitations and failure modes (such as full occlusions and computational cost).
weaknesses: High computational cost at inference: width-wise concatenation of reference latents doubles the token length in the DiT, resulting in roughly 7 minutes per 33-frame generation on an A100 GPU.

Because prior methods cannot take reference video effects directly, baselines are conditioned purely on text prompts (or static depth/pose plus text); the paper would be further strengthened by comparing against alternative reference injection mechanisms (e.g., cross-attention/IP-Adapter style conditioning) as architectural baselines.
Resolution and length are constrained to 33 frames at 15 fps and 480p, and the dataset is heavily human-centric, which currently limits applicability to broader open-world cinematic scenes.

strengths: Novel and practically relevant task formulation: While video style transfer and subject personalization have received considerable attention, general feed-forward transfer of dynamic, time-varying visual effects (VFX) from a reference video to an arbitrary target video has been largely under-explored.

Well-designed and scalable dataset construction pipeline: Since natural triplets of (reference effect, input video, output video) do not exist, the paper proposes a clever multi-source curation strategy combining LoRA-based image-to-video generation, a multi-stage synthetic V2V generation pipeline using pose/appearance guidance, and code-based programmatic effects on masked video datasets (totaling over 120K triplets across 1,700 effects).

Effective conditioning architecture and controllable inference: Extending the Wan2.1 DiT backbone via width-wise latent concatenation and formulating a multi-directional classifier-free guidance (CFG) scheme allows intuitive, continuous trade-offs between input fidelity and effect strength at test time.

Thorough evaluation: The authors conduct extensive 2AFC human preference studies (over 15,000 annotations) covering multiple dimensions (Reference Video Adherence, Input Video Adherence, and Overall Match), demonstrating consistent and statistically significant gains over baselines.
weaknesses: Asymmetric baseline comparison: Existing baselines (Wan2.1, Wan VACE, Lucy Edit) are primarily text-driven and do not natively accept reference video latents, meaning baselines are guided solely by text prompts describing the effect. While the paper includes an informative 'No Ref' ablation, exploring or adapting reference-guided video editing / style transfer baselines (e.g., using video-adapted IP-Adapter or visual prompting) would provide a more competitive reference-to-reference comparison.

High computational cost at inference: Concatenating full reference video latents width-wise effectively doubles the sequence length within the DiT blocks, leading to roughly 2x latency (~7 minutes per 33-frame clip on an A100 GPU), which somewhat limits interactive or real-time creative workflows.

Limitations in domain diversity and complex occlusions: As noted in the limitations, the training data and pipeline are heavily human- and foreground-centric. The model struggles with intricate physical interactions, full-body occlusions (e.g., submersion in water), and non-human environmental scenes.

strengths: Novel and practically relevant task formulation: While existing video editing frameworks focus heavily on text instructions or static visual appearance references (e.g., identity or style preservation), transferring temporally evolving dynamic effects from an unaligned reference video to a target video without test-time optimization is a compelling and underexplored setting.

Clever multi-source data generation pipeline: Since ground-truth video-to-video effect transfer triplets do not exist naturally, the paper introduces an automated curation pipeline combining LoRA-based image-to-video data, keyframe-edited and pose-guided synthetic video pairs, and programmatic spatio-temporal effects, generating a large-scale dataset of over 120K triplets across 1,700 effects.

Clean architectural integration: Adapting the diffusion transformer backbone (Wan2.1) by concatenating reference latents width-wise allows full self-attention across reference dynamics and target content without requiring disparate dual-branch architectures or complex feature injection modules.

Comprehensive subjective evaluation: The paper conducts an extensive user study comprising over 15,000 evaluations across 500+ annotators, broken down across multiple evaluation axes (Reference Video Adherence, Input Video Adherence, and Overall Match) with statistical bootstrap verification.
weaknesses: Asymmetric baseline comparison: Because existing video editing methods cannot directly ingest a reference video, baselines (Wan VACE Pose/Depth, Lucy Edit) are conditioned only on text prompts describing the effect. While an ablation ('No Ref') is included, this inherently gives the proposed method an informational advantage over the external baselines, making the win rates in user studies and embedding similarity metrics somewhat expected.

Heavy reliance on simplistic 2D programmatic effects: Out of the 120K training triplets, approximately 100K are generated via programmatic transitions and pixel-level filters (posterize, glitch, dither, wipe transitions). While reproducible, these make up the bulk of the dataset and differ substantially in complexity and realism compared to true photorealistic cinematic/physical temporal effects.

Domain bias in neural V2V pipeline: The scalable video-to-video generation pipeline fundamentally relies on subject pose extraction (DWPose/image-to-pose) and human-centric priors. As acknowledged in the limitations, this restricts training and generalization largely to human-centric foreground actions, leaving broader environmental, fluid, or generic object dynamics underrepresented.

Significant inference overhead: Concatenating the full reference video latents along the spatial width dimension doubles the token count processed by the DiT blocks, resulting in a roughly 2x increase in generation time (requiring ~7 minutes for a 33-frame 480p clip on an A100 GPU), which hinders practical adoption.

Lack of automated video fidelity metrics tailored to effect disentanglement: Relying primarily on global VideoPrism cosine similarity to input and reference videos conflates scene content similarity with dynamic effect fidelity; stronger quantitative validation isolating temporal dynamics from static appearance would strengthen the empirical claims.
